part_title: SageMaker Serving, Reliability and Bedrock Cross-Region Inference

scenes.title: Size a SageMaker Model Deployment
scenes.narration: When you deploy your own foundation model on Amazon SageMaker, model placement and instance choice matter. This diagram starts on the left with model artifacts stored in Amazon S3. The next box chooses a compatible inference container and instance class, taking into account whether the model needs a CPU or accelerator. The third stage creates and tests a SageMaker endpoint, which loads the model and performs health checks. Finally, an application sends inference requests and the team monitors real latency, error and utilization metrics. Notice the size decision panel on the right. Smaller CPU-compatible models may fit traditional CPU instances, while larger or accelerator-backed models need suitable hardware and memory. An instance that is too small can fail to load or run slowly; an oversized instance wastes money. Use model size, precision, batch size, measured concurrency and real traffic to select infrastructure. The key takeaway is to benchmark your actual serving configuration rather than treating the largest instance as automatically best.

scenes.title: Scale Large Models and Manage Endpoint Startup
scenes.narration: Large foundation models bring two separate challenges: making inference fit across enough accelerator memory, and managing startup time. On the left, the diagram shows a distributed accelerator topology. One model may be partitioned across several accelerators that communicate over a high-bandwidth interconnect. This can enable larger models or faster parallel execution, but it also introduces communication and placement constraints. On the right, the endpoint lifecycle goes through a request to deploy, orchestration, downloading model artifacts, loading model weights, health checks and finally a ready endpoint. Notice the highlighted startup-latency warning. Even when inference is fast once the model is warm, an endpoint can take significant time to load a large model and pass health checks. Monitor readiness separately from per-request inference latency, and design autoscaling with realistic startup delays. For production, test cold-start, rollback and failure recovery, not just the performance of one already warmed-up instance.

scenes.title: Retry Transient Failures with Backoff
scenes.narration: This slide illustrates a resilient retry policy for temporary errors. Step one sends an inference request. Step two receives a transient failure such as throttling or a server error. Instead of immediately retrying at full speed, step three waits for an exponentially increasing delay with randomized jitter. Step four retries within a configured attempt and total-time limit. Step five either succeeds or returns a controlled error when the budget is exhausted. Look at the lower timeline: the example delays grow from about one hundred to two hundred to four hundred milliseconds before jitter, but real values should follow the SDK and workload policy. The purple cards emphasize retrying only transient errors. Bad authentication, invalid inputs and permissions failures should not be blindly retried. Use AWS SDK retry configuration when appropriate, avoid duplicate effects for non-idempotent actions, and design a maximum attempt count. Jitter helps prevent thousands of clients from retrying in lockstep during an outage.

scenes.title: Reuse Connections for Efficient Inference
scenes.narration: Every unnecessary connection setup can add latency to an application calling Amazon Bedrock. Compare the two halves of this slide. On the left, each request constructs a new client and HTTP connection, repeating connection establishment and TLS handshakes. The pattern performs extra work even when the destination is unchanged. On the right, an application worker creates a supported SDK client once and reuses it across requests, allowing the HTTP connection pool to keep eligible connections warm. The numbered steps show client initialization, pool configuration, sending requests through the pool and handling stale connections correctly. The orange caution says that greater concurrency doesn't automatically improve throughput, because service quotas, model capacity and application resources still apply. Don't share mutable state unsafely between requests, and let the SDK manage connection lifetime where supported. The lesson is to remove avoidable setup overhead while preserving authorization, timeouts, retries and safe concurrent use.

scenes.title: Bedrock Cross-Region Inference
scenes.narration: This diagram shows a supported way to route inference capacity across AWS Regions. The application starts in its source Region and invokes a Bedrock inference profile rather than naming only one fixed destination. The Bedrock service may route the request to an eligible destination Region within the profile's allowed routing scope based on model availability and capacity. The model generates the response there, and the application receives it through the source Region's Bedrock endpoint. The world map in the centre is conceptual; actual routing Regions depend on the chosen inference profile. The lower boxes distinguish geographic profiles, which route within supported Regions in a specified geography, from global profiles, which can access a broader supported regional pool. Now look at the governance notes. IAM and service control policies must allow the profile and relevant destination Regions. Review data-residency requirements before allowing cross-Region routing. This technique can improve access to capacity, but it is not a guarantee that a particular Region will be chosen or that every request will be faster.

scenes.title: Choose the Right Inference Profile
scenes.narration: We conclude with a four-step decision guide. First, define the workload's permitted destinations, governance constraints and latency objectives. Second, choose an inference profile. The cyan panel on the right describes a geographic profile, which limits routing to supported Regions inside the selected geographical boundary. The orange panel describes a global profile, which permits a broader pool of supported Regions when policy allows it. Third, configure IAM permissions and any relevant organization service-control policies for the profile and its eligible destinations. Fourth, invoke and monitor actual latency, errors, throttling and cost. The comparison is not just geographic versus global branding: it is a question of where the request may be processed and which operational trade-offs are acceptable. The caution at the bottom reminds us that cross-Region inference does not guarantee a particular destination model's availability or a lower-cost request. Choose based on policy, supported routing and observed results. That completes Module Four's optimization cycle: measure, choose, cache, and improve.
